why: An FDE negotiates for a living - what is in the pilot and what is not, whether the go-live slips, whether that 'small ask' becomes a change order - so the offer negotiation is the first time the people who will staff you on accounts watch you hold a position under pressure with a real relationship on the line. Folding in ten minutes because a recruiter said 'this is the band' is the same behaviour that later turns a fixed-scope deployment into six months of unpaid feature work. FDE compensation is also structurally messier than a straight software engineering offer - hybrid or field ladders with different equity bands, travel load, on-call for someone else's production, sometimes a variable component tied to deployment milestones - so the highest-leverage moves here are structural (which ladder, which level, what is written down) rather than an extra few percent on base.
prerequisites: A live pipeline from topics 82 and 83 - a target list of ~40 companies and loops running in waves - because leverage in this topic is almost entirely a function of having real alternatives at the same time, not of technique.

Your narrative from topic 72 (why FDE, why this company, travel, comp): the compensation-expectations question lands in the first ten minutes of the first recruiter call, before any of this material gets a chance to matter.
Public proof from topics 69 and 80 - published case studies, working repos, recorded demos - which is the evidence you point at when you ask for a level review rather than just asserting seniority.
Executive communication from topic 68: a counter is a ninety-second, bottom-line-up-front ask delivered on a call, not a four-paragraph email.

Basic financial modelling in a spreadsheet: annualising a four-year grant, discounting by probability, and comparing two offers on year-one cash versus four-year total versus risk-adjusted expected value.

Honest, written knowledge of your own constraints before anyone asks: monthly burn, months of runway, notice period, dependents, relocation or visa limits, and what you are contractually leaving behind (unvested equity, an unpaid bonus, a clawback).

subtopics.name: The full surface area of an FDE offer
subtopics.learn: Enumerate every component before valuing any of them: base, target bonus (percentage of base, discretionary or contractual, pro-rated in year one), equity (RSU or option, dollar-denominated or share-denominated, and its vesting shape), sign-on cash (often split across two years, always attached to a clawback), relocation, and the FDE-specific lines - travel load, per-diem and booking policy, on-call stipend for customer production, region and account assignment, and in field orgs a variable or MBO component tied to deployment milestones. Learn who can move what: a recruiter can usually move sign-on and start date alone, the hiring manager owns level and scope, and base above band or an out-of-band grant needs a compensation committee exception that takes days. Learn that a dollar-denominated grant converts to shares at a price fixed on a specific date - grant date, or a trailing 15/20/30-day average - so 'X dollars of equity' can shrink materially between handshake and grant notice unless the conversion date is stated in writing.

resource.label: GitLab Handbook - Compensation: pay bands, levels, variable pay and the parts of an offer

subtopics.name: Calibrating a market band before anyone asks you for a number
subtopics.learn: Build a band from at least three independent sources per target company and write it down before the first call: levels.fyi percentiles filtered by company, level and metro; the posted range (several US states and cities require the range in the posting or on request, so 'what is the band for this level?' is a legitimate, answerable question); and two humans who actually hold the role. Record P25/P50/P75 separately for base, annualised equity and total comp rather than one blended figure, because the shape differs enormously - AI labs load equity, consultancies and services orgs load base plus variable. Know the data hazards: self-reported data skews high and skews toward the roles people brag about, private-company numbers go stale the moment the 409A moves, and FDE-style titles are thin in every dataset, so map the role onto the nearest engineering level and search that instead of the literal title. The output is three numbers per company - floor, target, stretch - that you read off a page later instead of inventing under pressure.

resource.label: The Pragmatic Engineer - The Trimodal Nature of Software Engineering Salaries

subtopics.name: Level and ladder: the FDE slotting problem
subtopics.learn: The highest-value negotiation in an FDE offer is usually structural, not numeric. Ask directly and early: is this role on the software engineering job family or on a separate field/solutions/services ladder, what is the internal level code, what are the bands for the level above and below, and what is the written promotion rubric. Field ladders frequently carry lower equity bands, slower or absent refresh cycles, and a ceiling one or two rungs below the engineering ladder, and moving ladders after you join is far harder than being slotted correctly on day one. Read live FDE and deployment-strategist postings side by side (Anthropic, Palantir, Databricks, OpenAI, Scale) and learn to spot the tells - 'solutions', 'delivery', 'resident' versus a posting that sits in the engineering job family with a stated level. Then learn the counter that actually works: not 'pay me more' but 'given the scope you described - owning a deployment end to end with no engineering backstop - this looks like your L5; here is the evidence, can you take it to the leveling committee?'

resource.label: Engineering Ladders - the Developer track, level by level (jorgef/engineeringladders)

subtopics.name: Walk-away, BATNA and ZOPA: four numbers set in writing first
subtopics.learn: Pre-commit four numbers before any conversation, because you cannot compute them honestly while a recruiter is on the phone: the walk-away (below which you decline and mean it), the target (a good outcome), the stretch (your opening ask), and the indifference point between your top two live options. Get the vocabulary right - your BATNA is your best alternative if this negotiation fails (stay put, take the other offer, keep interviewing with N live loops) and its quality, not your desire for the job, is what creates leverage; your reservation price is the worst deal you will still accept. Derive the walk-away from real inputs - twelve-month burn, notice-period gap, dependents, relocation and visa costs, unvested equity you forfeit, opportunity cost of loops you abandon - never from current salary plus a percentage. Learn ZOPA, the overlap between their maximum and your minimum, and accept that when there is no overlap the right move is a fast, warm no rather than a slow grind that burns a relationship you will want in three years.

resource.label: Harvard PON - What is BATNA? How to Find Your Best Alternative to a Negotiated Agreement

subtopics.name: Never the first number: deflection that survives three asks
subtopics.learn: Drill the deflection until it is boring, because whoever names a number first defines the range and the recruiter will ask inside the first ten minutes. Sequence: (1) 'I would rather get fit and level right first - what range is budgeted for this role?'; (2) 'I am sure you will be competitive; what does the band look like at that level?'; (3) if pressed a third time, give a researched total-comp range with an explicit dependency - 'somewhere in the X to Y range depending on level and how the equity is structured' - never a single point. Know the legal backdrop: many US states and cities prohibit asking for salary history at all, and several require disclosure of the posted range on request, so declining to share history is normal rather than adversarial. Never misstate your current or competing compensation - it is sometimes verifiable, it destroys the offer when caught, and the FDE community at these companies is small enough that it follows you. Talk about the market rate for the work, not about your history.

resource.label: Patrick McKenzie - Salary Negotiation: Make More Money, Be More Valued

subtopics.name: Sequencing the pipeline so two offers land in the same fortnight
subtopics.learn: Leverage is mostly a scheduling problem, and it is solved weeks before the offer call. Start the slowest processes first, put your top-choice company second rather than first so you arrive practised and with a live alternative, and slow the fast ones deliberately ('I have two processes finishing in a fortnight - can we align final rounds?'). Learn the honest accelerants: telling a company truthfully that you are in final stages elsewhere, asking a recruiter to compress a loop into one week, asking for a decision date rather than a number. Learn the recovery when timing fails and you have one offer with the rest at round two: convert the offer into a disclosed deadline for the others, accept that some processes will not move, and decide in advance whether you would take the bird in hand. Keep one table with company, stage, recruiter name, next date and expected decision date, because every move in this topic depends on knowing at any moment what your real alternatives are.

resource.label: Haseeb Qureshi - How to Break Into the Tech Industry: Job Hunting and Interviews

subtopics.name: Exploding offers and buying time
subtopics.learn: A 24- or 72-hour fuse is a pressure tactic far more often than a real constraint, and asking for time almost never costs you an offer - a company that has spent six weeks and several engineers' days on your loop does not rescind over a one-week extension. Learn the specific asks: a written extension with a concrete reason ('I have a final round on the 14th and I will not commit to something I cannot honour'), time with two more people on the team, and the equity plan documents plus grant notice, which legitimately take days to read. Learn to name the tactic politely if it persists, and to treat a flat refusal as data - a company that manufactures urgency with a candidate will do it to you with a customer deadline. Learn the mirror-image obligation: once you have decided, move within a day, because slow-rolling a company you intend to decline costs you a relationship in a small market.

resource.label: NACE - Advisory Opinion: Setting Reasonable Deadlines for Job Offers

subtopics.name: The counter: a prioritised package, delivered live
subtopics.learn: Structure the counter as a package with an explicit priority order, deliver it on a call, and confirm in writing afterwards - long email threads strip the tone and leave only the number. The shape that works: genuine enthusiasm and a specific reason you want this role, the constraint or alternative that justifies the ask, two or three requests with the most important named first, and a clear close ('if you can do X, I will sign today' - and only say that if it is true). Mechanics that matter: ask for the level review before anything else because it lifts every other number; counter on total compensation when the base band is rigid; use sign-on to bridge a gap the band cannot close, including bridging unvested equity you are forfeiting, and bring the vest schedule as evidence; never state a number you would not accept, because your ask is a commitment. When they say no, ask the two follow-ups that keep the conversation alive: 'what would have to be true for that to be possible?' and 'if the cash is fixed, can we move start date, sign-on, or the equity refresh at the first review?'

resource.label: Haseeb Qureshi - How Not to Bomb Your Offer Negotiation

subtopics.name: Tactical empathy and calibrated questions on a recruiter call
subtopics.learn: Take the three moves from Never Split the Difference that survive contact with a professional recruiter and drill only those: labels ('it sounds like the band is a real constraint on your side'), mirrors (repeating their last three words so they keep talking and reveal what is flexible), and calibrated how/what questions ('how am I supposed to make this work against an offer that pays materially more?') that hand them the problem without an ultimatum. Use the accusation audit for the awkward opening - 'you are probably going to think I am being difficult here' - and use silence after you make the ask, because the pause is where a recruiter fills in a concession. Learn explicitly what not to import: hostage-negotiation aggression, invented deadlines and manufactured scarcity read as amateurish, and they are unnecessary when your alternative is real.

resource.label: FBI Law Enforcement Bulletin - active listening skills: an evaluation tool for crisis negotiators

subtopics.name: Equity mechanics: strike, 409A, vesting shapes, cliffs, refresh, dilution
subtopics.learn: Learn the vocabulary well enough to interrogate a grant rather than admire it: RSU versus ISO versus NSO; strike price versus 409A fair market value versus last preferred price; grant date versus vesting commencement date; the standard four-year vest with a one-year cliff and monthly or quarterly vesting after, and the variants (back-loaded shapes such as 5/15/40/40 propped up by year-one and year-two cash bonuses, front-loaded grants, and one-year grants that are really an annual re-negotiation). Then learn the details that decide whether the paper is money: the post-termination exercise window (commonly 90 days, sometimes extended to seven or ten years), double-trigger RSUs at private companies that need both time vesting and a liquidity event before a seven-year expiry, the refresh grant policy and whether field roles are on the same refresh cadence as engineering, and dilution from future rounds. Learn the preference stack - a 1x non-participating preferred over a large raised total means a mediocre exit pays common holders nothing - and always ask for fully diluted shares outstanding so a percentage means something.

resource.label: The Open Guide to Equity Compensation (jlevy/og-equity-compensation)

subtopics.name: Valuing the equity: turning a headline into a defensible range
subtopics.learn: Build the spreadsheet that converts each grant into annual expected value plus a range, never a point estimate. Public RSUs: shares times current price, split across the actual vest schedule, with year one written as zero until the cliff and an explicit share-price assumption you can defend. Private options: (exit price per common share minus strike) times shares, times probability of exit, minus the cash required to exercise and the tax required to hold - then run three scenarios (down-round or acqui-hire where common gets nothing, 2x, 10x) and show all three. Refuse the two standard sleights of hand: valuing common at the last preferred price, and quoting a four-year grant total as though it were an annual number. Compare offers on three normalised axes - year-one cash, four-year total, and risk-adjusted expected value - and keep the assumptions visible next to each cell so you can defend the comparison out loud when a recruiter challenges your maths.

resource.label: Cooley GO - Liquidation preference: why common stock can be paid last

subtopics.name: Tax and net: what you actually keep
subtopics.learn: Comparing gross numbers across offer structures is how people take the worse deal. For US-structured offers: RSUs are ordinary income at vest, and supplemental withholding at the flat statutory rate (22% federal up to the $1M threshold, 37% above) routinely under-withholds high earners into an April bill; sell-to-cover versus net-settle changes your cash position. ISOs create no ordinary income at exercise but the spread is an alternative minimum tax preference item that can generate a large cash tax on shares you cannot sell; NSOs are taxed as ordinary income on the spread at exercise. An 83(b) election on restricted stock or an early exercise must be filed within 30 days of transfer and the deadline is not recoverable. Know that the 90-day post-termination exercise window plus that tax bill is what silently converts a large option grant into zero. Do the arithmetic per offer, and route anything consequential through an actual tax professional - your job is to know which questions to ask, not to self-file.

subtopics.name: Non-US and remote offer structures
subtopics.learn: If any target is an Indian entity, an international remote role or a contractor arrangement, learn the structure before you compare numbers. Indian offers are quoted as CTC, which bundles employer PF, gratuity accrual and a 'performance-linked' variable that is not guaranteed cash - strip it back to fixed monthly in-hand before you compare with a US total-comp figure. ESOPs from an Indian entity are typically taxed as a perquisite at exercise on the spread between fair market value and exercise price, then capital gains at sale, with a deferral regime for eligible startups; confirm the specifics with a chartered accountant rather than a blog. Notice period (30/60/90 days) is a negotiable start-date constraint and buyouts are a real ask. For remote or contractor roles, know the difference between employee and independent contractor treatment - who withholds, who pays employer-side taxes, what benefits and equity you do and do not get - because an eye-catching contractor day rate frequently nets less than a salaried offer.

resource.label: Income Tax Department, India - official portal

subtopics.name: Non-cash terms an FDE should negotiate harder than base
subtopics.learn: For a forward-deployed role, several non-cash terms are worth more over four years than the base delta you are arguing about. Negotiate and get in writing: expected travel percentage and cadence (three days a week on site is a different life from one week a month), who books and who approves, per-diem, whether loyalty points are yours, and the weekend-travel policy; region and account assignment, and what happens when your account is re-staffed; on-call expectations for customer production and whether there is a stipend or comp time; start date (a later start is often the cheapest concession they can give you); the date and criteria of your first performance and equity review, ideally at six months rather than the default annual cycle; and the internal mobility path to product engineering if the FDE org is a stepping stone for you. If a variable or MBO component exists, ask for the historical attainment distribution across the team and a guarantee or draw for the first two quarters while you ramp.

resource.label: Haseeb Qureshi - Ten Rules for Negotiating a Job Offer

subtopics.name: Reading the paperwork: clawbacks, IP assignment, notice and dispute clauses
subtopics.learn: Read the offer letter, the equity plan document and the grant notice as three separate contracts, because the offer letter is the least binding of them and the plan document is where the exercise window, the transfer restrictions, the company repurchase right and the change-of-control treatment actually live. Look specifically for: sign-on clawback terms (usually full or pro-rated repayment if you leave inside twelve months) and relocation repayment; the invention-assignment and outside-activities clauses, which matter a great deal to you because you have public repos and side projects - ask for a prior-inventions schedule listing them and a carve-out for work done on your own time and equipment; non-solicit and any non-compete (enforceability varies by jurisdiction and has been actively litigated); mandatory arbitration and class-action waivers; and the at-will language that makes every verbal promise revocable. The rule that saves you: anything a hiring manager promises - level, travel, region, a six-month review, a promotion timeline - is not real until it is in the letter, because managers change roles within a year.

resource.label: US FTC - Noncompete Rule and related materials

subtopics.name: The written negotiation plan and the decision matrix
subtopics.learn: Produce the deliverable: one document per top company with the researched band and its sources, your floor/target/stretch, the level you are asking for and the evidence for it, the exact opening sentence of your counter, your top three asks in priority order with a fallback for each, the concessions you will accept in return, and your walk-away with the arithmetic that produced it. Add a normalisation sheet that puts every live offer on the same axes - year-one cash, four-year total, risk-adjusted equity value, plus the non-cash terms - and a weighted decision matrix whose weights you set before any numbers arrive, so the choice is not made by whoever called last. Include the scripts for the four moments you will otherwise fumble: the expectations question, the 'what will it take to sign today' question, the extension request, and the decline. Pre-writing the plan is the entire point: everything in this topic is easy on paper and hard in a live twelve-minute call.

resource.label: Harvard PON - A Negotiation Preparation Worksheet: A Tool for Continuous Improvement

subtopics.name: Rehearsal and the close
subtopics.learn: Run at least six recorded role-plays with a friend playing a recruiter who has a written role card and instructions to push: the expectations question in the first five minutes, 'this is the top of the band', a 48-hour exploding deadline, 'we cannot move base but we can add equity', 'do you have a competing offer, and what are the numbers?', and 'what will it take for you to sign today?'. Score yourself on the recording for the things you cannot feel in the moment - did you name a number first, did you fill your own silence, did you apologise for asking, did you concede a dimension you had not planned to, how long between their objection and your capitulation. Then drill the close: accept verbally, ask for the full document set, re-read the grant notice for the share count and conversion date, sign, and only then decline the others personally and warmly, with a short reason and no auction-style gloating - those recruiters are the people who will source your next role.

resource.label: MIT OCW 15.665 Power and Negotiation - negotiation simulations and reflection assignments

outcomes: You can state, for each of your top ten target companies, a sourced band (P25/P50/P75 split into base, annualised equity and total), a target, a stretch and a walk-away number, with the arithmetic behind the walk-away written down.

You can deflect the compensation-expectations question three consecutive times on a recorded call without naming a number, without lying about current pay, and without sounding evasive - and then give a defended range if pressed a fourth time.

You can convert any option grant into a three-scenario expected-value range given strike, 409A FMV, last preferred price, fully diluted share count, preference stack and vesting shape, and name the inputs you would have to request to do it.
You can run a live counter that moves at least two dimensions beyond base - level review, sign-on, equity, start date, review timing - and closes with a commitment you are prepared to honour.
You can name the level and ladder a given FDE offer sits on, the bands for the adjacent levels, and the promotion rubric, and can make an evidence-backed case for a level review to a hiring manager.

You can explain the after-tax difference between an RSU offer and an ISO grant of nominally equal headline value, including flat supplemental withholding shortfall, AMT on the exercise spread, and the 30-day 83(b) window.

You can find, in an offer letter and equity plan document, the six clauses that materially change the deal - sign-on clawback, exercise window, invention assignment, non-solicit, arbitration, change-of-control treatment - and articulate what you would ask to change in each.

You can choose between two competing offers using a matrix whose weights you set before the numbers arrived, and decline the loser in a three-sentence call that keeps the recruiter relationship intact.
failureModes: You give a number in the first recruiter screen, the whole process gets calibrated to it, and you never learn that the band topped out 35% higher because nobody had a reason to tell you.

You hint at a competing offer you do not have, the recruiter asks a specific follow-up about the level and structure, and the resulting stumble costs you both the credibility and the offer in a field small enough that people compare notes.

You win a 6% base bump and accept the level as offered, so you sit two years under a lower ceiling with smaller refreshes, and the promotion you were verbally promised needs a committee packet nobody prepared.

You compare a Series B option grant against public RSUs by multiplying shares by the last preferred price, ignoring strike, the liquidation preference and future dilution, and discover at an acqui-hire three years later that common holders received nothing.

The hiring manager promises a specific region, a travel ceiling and a six-month equity review on a call, none of it enters the offer letter, and eleven months in you are on a different account, travelling four days a week, reporting to someone who never heard the promise.

You take a sign-on bonus with a full twelve-month clawback, the deployment turns out to be staff-augmentation work with no engineering ownership, and leaving in month eight now costs you cash you have already spent.

You negotiate entirely over email, your carefully framed package arrives at the compensation committee as a single bald number with no justification, and the answer comes back as a flat no you have no conversational room to reopen.
interviewQuestions: Recruiter screen, minute six: 'So that we do not waste each other's time - what are your compensation expectations for this role?' Answer it out loud, and then I am going to ask you the same thing twice more.
You have our offer and one from a competitor. Tell me what it would take for you to sign with us today - and be specific, because I have to take it to a committee and defend it.

Walk me through how you would compare two offers where one is a public company paying RSUs and the other is a Series C paying options. What do you need to know about the Series C before you can even put the two on the same page, and how would you present that comparison to your partner at home?
We cannot move base - it is the top of the band for this level. But I can add equity. Talk me through what you would want to know before you decide whether that is a good trade for you.

A customer's VP tells you two weeks before go-live that the deployment is unacceptable without a feature that is not in the SOW, and threatens to escalate to your VP. You cannot deliver it and hold the date. How do you run that conversation, and what do you actually say first?

You accepted our offer three weeks ago. During onboarding you discover you were slotted one level below what the hiring manager described in the loop, and the equity in the grant notice is 20% below what the letter implied because of the conversion date. What do you do, in what order, and with whom?

Tell me about a negotiation you lost - with an employer, a vendor or a customer. What did you concede too early, what would you set as your walk-away if you ran it again, and how would you know in the moment that you were about to fold?
proofOfWork: Build a negotiation dossier for your live pipeline and keep it as a private, versioned artifact you can walk an interviewer through. It has four parts. First, a comparison model - a spreadsheet with one row per live or target company and columns for sourced band and its three sources, level and ladder, year-one cash, four-year total, risk-adjusted equity expected value under three exit scenarios with the assumptions visible, and the non-cash terms priced explicitly (travel days per year, on-call weeks, notice-period gap, forfeited unvested equity); every private-company row must compute from strike, 409A FMV, fully diluted shares and the preference stack rather than a headline number. Second, a one-page plan per top-five company containing your floor, target and stretch, the level you will ask for with the two pieces of public evidence you will cite, the literal first three sentences of your counter, your three asks in priority order with a fallback for each, and the walk-away with its arithmetic. Third, six recorded role-play sessions - each under fifteen minutes, each with a written role card for the counterparty covering a different pressure move (expectations question, top-of-band refusal, exploding deadline, equity-for-base swap, competing-offer probe, sign-today close) - plus a self-scored rubric per recording tracking whether you named a number first, seconds of silence you filled, dimensions conceded that were not in the plan, and time from objection to capitulation, with a visible trend across the six. Fourth, a clause-by-clause annotation of one real offer letter and one real equity plan document (redact the employer) marking the sign-on clawback, exercise window, vesting shape and conversion date, invention-assignment and outside-activities language, non-solicit, arbitration and change-of-control treatment, with the specific redline you would request on each. Once the negotiation actually happens, add a two-page delta memo: what you asked for, what you got, what you left on the table, which sentence changed the outcome, and what you will do differently next time - that memo is the part that turns a lucky outcome into a repeatable skill.
